passage: On Monday, Uday dropped the steel tumbler and milk splashed across the kitchen floor. Papa's voice from the next room was already booming, "What was that?" Uday whispered, "Not me," and hid behind the door, his heart pounding. On Wednesday he cracked a plate and slid the pieces under the cupboard. On Saturday, a new plate slipped and broke. Papa Harsha came in quietly and said, "I would rather know than have a broken plate hidden. I won't shout at you." Uday's hands trembled. He took a slow breath and said, "It was me." Papa nodded and knelt down to help him sweep.

qa.q: Where did Uday hide the pieces of the cracked plate?
qa.a: Uday slid the pieces under the cupboard.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling on Monday when he said "Not me"?
qa.a: Uday was afraid of Papa's booming voice. The fear was bigger than his wish to be honest, so he hid behind the door with a pounding heart.

qa.q: What changed on Saturday that let Uday tell the truth?
qa.a: Papa Harsha stayed quiet and promised not to shout, so telling felt safe. Safe truth-telling at home makes children more honest.

qa.q: How might Papa Harsha have seen Uday's hiding on Wednesday?
qa.a: Papa may have wondered why Uday hid things instead of telling him. The hiding may be a sign that Uday was scared, not simply naughty.

grounding: A child lies because he fears being scolded, the fear stronger than the wish to be honest, until a parent makes truth safe.

passage:
"Sarita, why is your school book torn?"
"I don't know, Amma. A boy did it."
"Which boy?"
Sarita twisted her frock. "A... new boy."
Lakshmi knelt down. "You're shaking. Are you scared I'll shout?"
Sarita nodded. "Last time you shouted so loud."
Lakshmi was quiet. "I did. I'm sorry. I don't want you to be scared to tell me things. In this house, truth is safe. What happened?"
"I pulled it from the shelf and it ripped."
"Thank you. We'll tape it together."

qa.q: What had happened to Sarita's school book?
qa.a: It was torn; she pulled it from the shelf and it ripped.

qa.q: Why did Sarita blame a new boy?
qa.a: She was scared her Amma would shout loudly again, and the fear was bigger than wanting to be honest.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi change to make truth feel safe?
qa.a: She noticed Sarita's fear, apologised for shouting last time, said truth is safe at home and responded calmly.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi feel when Sarita says "Last time you shouted so loud"?
qa.a: She may feel a pang of guilt and realise her shouting is teaching Sarita to hide things.

grounding: A young girl lies because she fears being shouted at, and her mother makes the truth feel safe.

passage:
From Aadhya's class teacher, to her mother, Kalyani.
Today Aadhya spilt green paint on her new white uniform. When I asked, she said Meera did it, though I saw it happen. Then she went pale and whispered, "Please don't tell Mummy. She'll scold me so much." I told her accidents are okay and she is not in trouble with me. We washed it together. When I stopped asking who did it and said she was safe, she said, "It was me." I'm writing so we can both make telling the truth feel safe for her.

qa.q: What did Aadhya spill on her uniform?
qa.a: She spilt green paint on her new white uniform.
She was afraid of being scolded at home, and the fear was bigger than her wish to be honest.

qa.q: What helped Aadhya finally say "It was me"?
qa.a: The teacher said accidents are okay and that she was safe, which took away the fear of punishment.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel reading this note?
qa.a: She may feel sad that Aadhya is so scared of her scolding, and want to make it safer to tell the truth at home.

grounding: A young girl lies about a paint spill because she fears being scolded, and admits it once the teacher makes it safe.
